title: Conditional probability from a tree diagram
log: 2026-11-04T09:36:55Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new

match.reason: The closest bank point, Multi-stage experiments, covers tree diagrams without replacement and multiplying along paths, but it never teaches that second-stage branches are conditional probabilities, which is the central idea of the new point, and the conditional probability cards teach the P(A|B) formula and tables rather than tree diagrams.

draft.title: Conditional probability from trees
card: In a tree diagram without replacement, the first branches show the chance of the first outcome. Nothing is put back, so the counts change.
The second branches show probabilities given the first outcome. Use the new total and the new count after the first pick.
Multiply along a path to get the chance of both outcomes happening in that order.
Example: a bag has 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two are drawn without replacement. P(red then red) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 6/20 = 3/10.
draft.remember: Second branches are given the first pick. Multiply along a path for the combined chance.

a.q: A bag has 4 green and 3 yellow counters. One green is drawn and not replaced. What is P(green on the second draw | green first)?
a.why: After one green is removed, 3 green and 3 yellow remain, so there are 6 counters and 3 are green. 4/7 ignores the first draw.
a.clue: Count what is left in the bag after the first draw.

b.q: A box has 5 milk and 3 dark chocolates. Mia eats two at random, one after the other. What is P(milk then dark)?
b.why: P(milk first) = 5/8. Then 7 remain, 3 of them dark, so 3/7. Multiply: 5/8 × 3/7 = 15/56. 15/64 forgets that one chocolate has been eaten.
b.clue: Multiply along the path, using the new total for the second branch.

check.summary: No problems found. Both answers check out (3/6 and 15/56), the card's example is correct, and the explanations match the card.
